Help eliminate unquoted path vulnerabilities Published: 2012-11-07 Last Updated: 2012-11-08 04:05:52 UTC by Mark Baggett (Version: 1) 19 comment(s) Metasploit\xe2\x80\x99s \xe2\x80\x9cService Trusted Path Privilege Escalation\xe2\x80\x9d exploit takes advantage of unquoted service paths vulnerability outline in CVE-2005-1185, CVE=2005-2938 and CVE-2000-1128.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 The vulnerability takes advantage of the way Windows parses directory paths to execute code.\xc2 \xc2 Consider the following command line. C:\\windows\\system32\\notepad \\temp\\file.txt This tells windows to launch notepad.exe from the c:\\windows\\system32\\ directory and pass it the argument \\temp\\file.txt.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 The result is notepad.exe will execute and begin editing file.txt from the temp directory.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 How does Window\xe2\x80\x99s differentiate between the program and the arguments?\xc2 The SPACE is used as a delimiter between the program to execute and the arguments.\xc2 \xc2 Now consider this command line. C:\\program files\\Microsoft Office\\Winword.exe If space is used as a delimiter, wouldn\xe2\x80\x99t Windows think you are trying to execute the program\xc2 C:\\PROGRAM.EXE and pass it the argument \xe2\x80\x9cfiles\\Microsoft Office\\Winword.exe\xe2\x80\x9d?\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Or maybe you are trying to execute \xe2\x80\x9cC:\\Program files\\Microsoft.exe\xe2\x80\x9d and pass it the argument \xe2\x80\x9cOffice\\Winword.exe\xe2\x80\x9d?\xc2 So how does it know what you are trying to do?\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 If the software developer places quotation marks around the path then Windows knows the spaces are spaces and not delimiters.\xc2 \xc2 If the software developer fails to put the path in quotes then Windows just doesn\xe2\x80\x99t know.\xc2 If Windows doesn\xe2\x80\x99t know then it tries to execute all the possible programs in the path.\xc2 First it tries \xe2\x80\x9cC:\\Program.exe\xe2\x80\x9d,\xc2 \xc2 Then, it tries \xe2\x80\x9cC:\\Program files\\Microsoft.exe\xe2\x80\x9d and finally the path we intended for it to execute.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 This programming error is very common because when a developer is addressing paths on the file system they are usually stored in strings.\xc2 \xc2 Because they are in strings the developer has used quotes once already and they often fail to consider that they need two sets of quotes.\xc2 For example, the following line would incorrectly assign the path variable. pathvariable = \xe2\x80\x9cC:\\Program Files\\Common Files\\Java\\Java Update\\jusched.exe\xe2\x80\x9d Really, the developer needs to double quote it because they need the path to contain quotes.\xc2 So they should have assigned their variable by doing something like this: pathvariable = \xe2\x80\x9c\\\\\xe2\x80\x9dC:\\Program Files\\Common Files\\Java\\Java Update\\jusched.exe\\\\\xe2\x80\x9d\xe2\x80\x9d In the first case, an attacker can strategically place a program in the path and his program will be executed instead of the intended program.\xc2 \xc2 If the process runs under administrative privileges or some account other than the attacker it can be used to cause code to execute under a different set of privileges. \xc2 We have known about these types of vulnerabilities for 12 years now.\xc2 So much so, that if you create a file called c:\\program.exe Windows will generate this pop up when you reboot the machine. With such an old vulnerability, surely very few programs suffer from this problem, right?\xc2 You might be surprised at how often this vulnerability occurs.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 \xc2 So let\xe2\x80\x99s start fixing it!\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 This is an easy problem to identify.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Here are some steps you can follow to identify applications that fail to quote their file paths directly.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Then you can help fix this by contacting the vendor to have them fix these issues. First you need to copy any existing executable and create a program named c:\\program.exe.\xc2 \xc2 For example, take a copy of calc.exe and name it c:\\program.exe.\xc2 \xc2 Then make a copy of calc.exe named c:\\program files\\common.exe.\xc2 Last, create a copy of calc.exe called c:\\documents.exe.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Then go about your business and use your computer as you normally would.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Sometime while you are running normal applications they will accidently launch the renamed calc.exe.\xc2 \xc2 System reboots, services and scheduled tasks may trigger calculator.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Whatever the cause, eventually you will likely run a vulnerable program and it will launch the application on your computer.\xc2 \xc2 Several days may transpire between the time you create the files and the time they are executed.\xc2 \xc2 Remember you did this when you have strange copies of calc.exe spontaneously launching on your computer.\xc2 \xc2 Once one your copy of calculator executes, first find out which one of your calc.exe programs launched and who launched it.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Use WMIC to query which copy of your calculator is running like this. Here you can see this query for \xe2\x80\x9cprogram.exe\xe2\x80\x9d returns the command line that was executed when our executable launched.\xc2 \xc2 This program failed to properly quote the system paths and launched your renamed program.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 Often times you may be able to identify the vendor responsible for the software from just the command line that launched your program.\xc2 \xc2 \xc2 \xc2 But often times it is also useful to know the parent process that launched the command line that started your program.\xc2 \xc2 To find out what program launched the unquoted path we use the following commands. There you go bug hunter.\xc2 You found a 0-Day vulnerability!\xc2 Now notify the vendor so they can patch it and keep everyone safe.\xc2 While you are at it you can notify us if you would like.
